Krosniewice Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Krośniewice, Poland

Not demolished. Krośniewice, a private town founded in 1452, saw Jewish settlement first mentioned in 1564, initially under Łęczyca's kehilla before independence in 1765 (79 residents). Population grew to 5,054 (43%) by 1897, settling around 1,300 by the interwar period. A May 1940 ghetto grew from 1,500-1,600 to 2,000 residents within three months; its 1942 liquidation deported survivors to Chełmno. This cemetery, likely established in the first half of the 19th century (documented existing by 1864), had its matzevot used for road and sidewalk paving during WWII; Poland formally began closure proceedings September 25, 1965. Restoration in 1999 (funded by Abraham Levy of Israel) added a small lapidary; a more extensive 2014 effort by former resident Sol Rosenkranz, with support from the Foundation for the Preservation of Jewish Heritage and the US Commission for the Preservation of America's Heritage Abroad, fenced the site and unveiled a memorial that August. A 2015 access road followed, and a 2017 cleanup marking the 75th anniversary of the Krośniewice Jews' murder recovered two more matzevah fragments found during nearby street renovation.
